timeline: Balkh, the year one thousand and thirty two. A gallows stands outside the city. The man they bring to it was, not long ago, the most powerful minister in the empire. And when it was over, he was left alone, just as alone as he had come from his mother's womb.

Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio One. Every week, I open a book that was written nearly a thousand years ago, in Persian, by a man who made his readers a promise. He promised to write only what he had seen with his own eyes, or heard from people he trusted.
His name was Abolfazl Beyhaqi, and today, I want to tell you the story that made him famous.
It is the story of a vizier named Hasanak. A powerful man, a proud man, and, in the end, a man standing alone on a gallows in the city of Balkh.

Let me take you to the beginning of the eleventh century. In the east of the Persian world, in what is today Afghanistan, there was a great empire ruled from the city of Ghazni. Its king was Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, one of the most famous rulers of his age. His armies marched as far as India. Poets filled his court.
And next to him, managing the endless business of the empire, stood his vizier, his chief minister: Hasanak.

Hasanak came from a respected family of Nishapur. He was young for such a high position, clever, wealthy, and very sure of himself. When you are the right hand of the most powerful king in the region, it is easy to believe the world will always be on your side.

But Sultan Mahmud had two sons. One was Muhammad, the son he favored. The other was Masud, a strong and ambitious prince who did not always get along with his father. And Hasanak made a choice that seemed safe at the time. He stood with the father, and with Muhammad, and he did not hide his contempt for Masud.

Beyhaqi tells us that Hasanak once said something sharp and insulting about Masud, words along the lines of: if Masud ever becomes king, let them hang me. People at court remembered it. People at court always remember.

There was a second problem. Years earlier, Hasanak had gone on the pilgrimage to Mecca. On the way back, he did not return the usual way. He passed through Egypt, which was ruled by the Fatimid caliphs, the great rivals of the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. In Egypt, Hasanak accepted a robe of honor from the Fatimid court.

To us, that may sound like a simple gift. But in that world, it was politics. The caliph in Baghdad was furious. To him, accepting honors from the Fatimids looked like loyalty to his enemies, and his letters began to call Hasanak a heretic, a Qarmatian, a word that in those days could cost a man his life.
Sultan Mahmud, it is said, protected his vizier and brushed the accusations aside. As long as Mahmud lived, Hasanak was safe.
And then, in the year 1030, Sultan Mahmud died.

What followed was a short and bitter struggle between the brothers. Muhammad was placed on the throne first, but he did not last. Masud, the son Hasanak had insulted, won. He became Sultan. And suddenly, everything that Hasanak had said and done came back to the surface.

Hasanak was arrested. And at court there was a man who had been waiting for this moment for a long time. His name was Bu Sahl Zuzani. Beyhaqi does not hide his opinion of him. He describes Bu Sahl as a man with a cruel streak, someone who enjoyed watching great men fall, and who had an old grudge against Hasanak.

Bu Sahl pressed the new Sultan again and again. The caliph in Baghdad wants this man punished, he said. He is a heretic. He insulted you. Masud, Beyhaqi suggests, hesitated. But the pressure, the letters from Baghdad, and the old insult were too much.

Before the end, there was a hearing. Hasanak was brought before the new chief minister, an old and experienced statesman named Ahmad Hasan Maymandi. Hasanak had lost everything: his office, his wealth, his freedom. Beyhaqi describes him arriving in plain clothes, a man who had once dressed like a prince.

And here Beyhaqi gives us one of the most human scenes in the whole book. When Hasanak was brought in, the old minister treated him with respect. Not as a prisoner, but as a man who had once held the same office. Bu Sahl, watching, was furious and began to insult Hasanak in front of everyone.
And the old minister turned on Bu Sahl and silenced him. Whatever this man has done, he was saying, you do not humiliate a fallen man. Not in my presence.
Hasanak, for his part, did not beg. He answered calmly and with dignity. He knew how this would end.

The execution took place in the city of Balkh, in the year 1032. A gallows was set up near the city. Hasanak was led out, his head covered. Beyhaqi tells us that people had been paid to throw stones at him, as was the custom with those condemned as heretics. But almost no one did.
The crowd stood there, and many of them wept.

And then Beyhaqi writes one of the most famous lines in Persian prose. I'll say it in Persian, and then in English. Hasanak tanha mand, chenanke tanha amade bud az shekam-e madar. Hasanak was left alone, just as alone as he had come from his mother's womb.
His body, Beyhaqi says, remained on the gallows for about seven years.
There is one more person in this story, and for many readers she is the true hero. Hasanak's mother.

When the news was brought to her, the people around her expected screaming, collapse, curses. Instead, she was silent for a moment, and then she said something that Persian speakers still quote a thousand years later. In Beyhaqi's words, she said: what a great man my son was.
A king like Mahmud gave him this world, and a king like Masud gave him the next.
Think about that. In one sentence, she refused to let the powerful decide what her son's life meant. They had taken his body. They would not take his dignity.
So why did Beyhaqi, a young secretary who worked for this same Sultan Masud, write all of this down?

That is the part I love most. Beyhaqi wrote his history years later, after Masud himself was gone. He could have flattered the dynasty he served. Instead, he wrote that Hasanak's death was unjust, that Bu Sahl was driven by spite, and that the crowd in Balkh wept.

He even tells us, more or less, why he is telling us: so that those who read this will learn that power does not last, that the world turns, and that a man is remembered for how he behaves when everything is taken from him.

That is why I call him The Honest Historian. In an age when most chroniclers wrote to please kings, Beyhaqi wrote to tell the truth. And he gave us, almost by accident, some of the most beautiful Persian prose ever written.
Next week, we'll stay at the court of Ghazni and meet the new Sultan, Masud himself: a brave, impulsive, complicated king, and the long road that took him from rebel prince to ruler of an empire.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
